1:
All four who raise it date the story early, against its place in the book. Gill says these chapters record facts done not after Samson’s death, as their order may suggest, but before any of the judges, between the death of Joshua and the rise of Othniel; they account for how idolatry got into Dan and spread over all the tribes, and so for the servitude that followed. Keil makes the point structurally: chapters 17 to 21 are appendices attached to a book whose body closes with Samson, and their facts belong to the very commencement of the times of the judges. Ellicott corrects the Latin reading, there was at that time — an error, for these events happened before the days of Samson. Only Clarke hesitates: the chronology is extremely difficult to fix, and all that can be said with certainty is that it happened when there was no king in Israel.

Ellicott presses the name. Micayehu means who is like Jehovah, and seems to show the man had been trained by pious parents, though Scripture says nothing more of him. He also states the thesis governing the episode: this was not worship of other gods but worship of the true God under unauthorised conditions and with forbidden images — a violation not of the first commandment but of the second.

Henry alone works the family quarrel. The son robs the mother, who had hoarded with long scraping and saving, and it did her good to count it over; a parent’s withholding what is meet will not excuse children who think all their own that they can get from them. Then the mother curses, so loud and with such vehemence as made both his ears tingle. See what mischief the love of money makes: her silver was her god before ever it was made a graven image, else its loss would not have put her into such a passion. Outward losses drive good people to their prayers, but bad people to their curses; and it is foolish for the provoked to throw curses about like a madman casting firebrands, since they may light on those dearest to them. Clarke and Ellicott make the curse a legal act rather than a passion: it is literally an adjuration, the one commanded in Leviticus, and Micah was terrified into confession lest it fall on him. He shows throughout, Ellicott adds, a singular mixture of superstition and ignorance.

Clarke defends the mother’s intention: she had no idolatrous design, for she expressly says she dedicated the silver to Jehovah, and that is why she cursed whoever took it. Ellicott leaves the grammar open — consecrating, I consecrated may mean she does so now in thanksgiving for its restoration, or had done so before it was stolen — but will not let the words pass: the terms for graven and molten image are the very ones used in the curse against idolaters in Deuteronomy. Whether they name one image or two he thinks impossible to determine, some taking them together for one silver image adorned with sculptured work. Gill notes that Micah returned the money a second time, not disapproving the intention, as the sequel shows, but to be rid of it. Two hundred of the eleven hundred shekels went to the founder. Ellicott reports the suggestion that this was the fifth part owed as trespass-money, rejects it because the sum will not come out, and concludes the rest was spent on other parts of the worship; he compares the two hundred pounds paid in penance by the murderers of a man killed in Westminster Abbey, which went on a costly image. Clarke will only say what these images were cannot positively be known, most probably some resemblance of things belonging to the tabernacle; Keil takes the words about restoring the silver as a repetition, a link to what it was finally used for.
5:
Beth Elohim reads two ways, and the reading decides how bad the chapter is. Gill takes it as a house of gods, there being two images in it besides teraphim, and notes the Targum has a house of images; but he allows it may be rendered a house of God, a place of worship. Clarke will have only the second: it should be translated house or temple of God, for it is very likely mother and son intended no more than a private chapel in which to set up the worship of the true God. Ellicott says the Hebrew means either equally well, and refuses to choose, because both are true at once. It is quite clear, he writes, that Micah did not abandon the worship of God under the names by which he was known to Israel; how he squared that with his grossly idolatrous symbols it is impossible to say. The fact remains that in Micah’s house we find a whole chapel of idols consecrated to Jehovah as a pious act.

Clarke reconstructs the chapel item by item, and the reconstruction is his own. Micah built it in imitation of the sanctuary: a graven image to represent the ark, a molten image the mercy-seat, teraphim the cherubim above it, and an ephod in imitation of the sacerdotal garments; then he consecrated a son to be priest. Gross idolatry was therefore not his crime; he only set up in his own house an epitome of the worship performed at Shiloh. He knows the Targum is against him, rendering the word for priest here by the term it reserves for an idolatrous one and keeping another for a priest of the true God; but this was not idolatry, he answers, since the divine name is used of the dedication and oracular answers were afterwards given at this house.

On the furniture the others are drier. Ellicott thinks the ephod no more than a gorgeous priestly garment, though possibly used for oracles; Keil calls it an imitation of the high priest’s shoulder-dress. The teraphim Keil takes for household gods, worshipped as givers; Ellicott traces them from the images Rachel stole down to the reformation that put them away, and reports that the old versions render them by words pointing to idolatrous images or the implements of necromancy. Both correct the English of consecrated: the Hebrew is to fill the hand, which Ellicott says means giving a man the office by putting certain offerings into his hands, and is rather installed. Keil adds a point of grammar with consequences for the story: the man Micah stands at the head of the verse absolutely, the whole verse being a circumstantial clause explaining what went before, so its verbs are pluperfects — the mother made her image because her son already had a house of God and a son officiating in it.

Then the refrain. Gill takes no king to mean no supreme magistrate, Joshua and Caleb and their contemporaries being dead. Clarke agrees that the word for king is sometimes used of a supreme governor, judge or magistrate, and draws the moral out: every man was his own governor, and what he did he called right, defending it by cunning and strength; when a man’s own will, passions and caprice are made the rule of law, society is in a most perilous and ruinous state, for civil government is of God, and without it the earth must soon be desolated. He then turns it on his own country: there was a time when there was no king in England, and that was in general a time of scandal to religion and oppression to men. Ellicott alone hears the refrain as evidence of date: it shows these narratives were written, or more probably edited, in the days of the monarchy, and explains why no prince or ruler interfered to prevent idolatrous or lawless proceedings.
7:
Ellicott drops the fact that changes the weight of the story: later on, as it were incidentally, we make the astonishing discovery that this young man was no other than a grandson of Moses. The rest of his note is quieter. Bethlehem is called of Judah to distinguish it from the one in Zebulun, as Gill also observes; in later times, when it was famous as David’s birthplace, the addition is often dropped. He also hears the sentence about sojourning against the old curse on Levi, that they should be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel.

What of the family of Judah attaches to is unsettled. Clarke offers two ways: family may be taken for tribe, or the young man might have been of Judah by his mother and of Levi by his father, since a Levite might marry into any tribe provided the woman was not an heiress. Ellicott doubts whether the phrase belongs to the young man or to Bethlehem, and notes that some manuscripts leave it out; if it does belong to him, it means he did not live in one of the Levitical cities of his own family, which lay in the northern and eastern tribes, but in Judah, and so was reckoned in civil matters to that tribe. Keil presses the point from the other side: Bethlehem was not a Levitical town, and the man was neither born there nor made a citizen of it, but simply sojourned.

Why he was on the road is the real question, and Henry puts both answers and refuses neither. It may have been his unhappiness: God had made plentiful provision for the Levites, but the people withheld their dues and did not help them into the cities assigned them, so they were reduced to straits and no care was taken for their relief. Israel’s forsaking God began with forsaking the Levites, and it is a sign religion is decaying when good ministers are neglected and at a loss for a livelihood. But it seems rather to have been his fault and folly, that he loved to wander, threw himself out where he was, forfeited the respect of his friends, and with a roving head would go seek his fortune. As those are fit to be pitied that would fix but may not, so those are fit to be punished that might fix but will not. Gill offers the same pair without deciding — a man of unsettled mind who could not easily fix anywhere, or a Levite driven abroad because no supreme magistrate made a negligent people pay their tithes. Clarke keeps to the economics: he sought employment about the country, for the Levites had no inheritance, and no secure residence could be found where there was no civil government. Ellicott supplies a parallel from a later century, when the portions of the Levites were not given them and the singers who did the work had fled every one to his field.

Micah’s side of the meeting Henry reads as slackness rather than piety. He was furnishing himself with a chaplain, having thought his own son either too good to officiate, as heir of the estate, or rather, not being of God’s tribe, not good enough. Had he been unhappy with his son as priest he would have sent abroad to seek out a Levite; instead he takes hold of one who drops into his hands, which showed he had no great zeal in the matter. As for the Levite, Henry thinks he had probably heard in the country of Micah’s house of gods and his graven image, and Ellicott agrees he was drawn there by the rumour of the chapel and its worship. Gill leaves the exchange at its plainest: a traveller might ask for a meal or a night’s lodging, and it was natural to ask whence he came and where he was going.
10:
Father is a title, not a relation. Clarke glosses the offer: thou shalt be master of my house, as if thou wert my father, and as priest shalt appear in the presence of God for me — the term being often used to express honour and reverence. Ellicott makes it technical: the title is here ecclesiastical, like papa or pope, given to spiritual directors elsewhere in Scripture. He adds that Micah knew enough of the law to know the irregularity of making his own son a priest.

The wage divides them, and the difference is not arithmetic but tone. Clarke reckons ten shekels at about thirty shillings a year, with board, lodging and clothes, and calls it very good wages in those early times. Ellicott reckons twenty-five, and turns the sum into an indictment: thus the grandson of Moses became priest of an idolatrous worship at a salary of twenty-five shillings a year. On the smaller words Ellicott is quieter: by the year is literally by days, and the suit of apparel is a double robe in the Latin, which he thinks means an order of garments or the value of them.

That the Levite stayed surprises nobody. Gill says he continued after trial, liking his service, wages and way of living; Clarke, that he thought the place a good one and the wages respectable. Only Ellicott hears a warning in the clause that the young man was unto him as one of his sons: the words are added, he says, in reflection on his subsequent ingratitude. On the installing, Gill notes that Micah invested him as he had consecrated his son before, by filling his hand with sacrifices; Clarke explains the idiom the same way, that he gave him an offering to present before the Lord, appointing him priest while leaving God to accept him. Keil sets the three verses down together, the contentment, the consecration and the confidence, as one movement.

Micah’s closing confidence draws the chapter’s sharpest disagreement, and Clarke defends him at length. Having provided an epitome of the tabernacle, a model of the ark, mercy-seat and cherubim, proper vestments and a Levite to officiate, he took for granted all was right; some think he expected gain from a concourse of people, but of this there is no evidence in the text. Micah and his mother appear not only perfectly sincere but perfectly disinterested, putting themselves to considerable expense to erect the place and maintain a priest at their own charges — without which it would in all probability have been destitute of the worship and knowledge of the true God. Given the state of the land, the profligacy of his countrymen and his distance from Shiloh, he deserves more praise than blame, though of the latter he has had a most liberal share from every quarter — which Clarke ascribes to the propensity in man to take another’s character by the worst handle; and he owns his own lean, saying it can be no crime if these notes are found leaning the other way. Ellicott will not go there. We are hardly placed to know whether the anticipation was hypocrisy or mere ignorance; and so far as Micah was sincere, we must feel that the Lord did him good by stripping him of his gorgeous instruments of superstition and humbling his pride. He reads the article too — not a Levite but the Levite, the man having as a son of Gershom a special right to represent the tribe — and insists Micah could hardly have been unaware that Levites were incapable of priestly functions, or that authorised worship belonged to the place God should choose, which was Shiloh. The passage is fresh proof of the utter neglect of the law from a very early period, and this house of God resembles the high places even faithful kings were unable or unwilling to clear away.
